We propose a generative framework that aligns paired multimodal recordings in a unified representation space and generates modality-specific haemodynamic responses from EEG. In paired cohorts, the framework generated fMRI BOLD and fNIRS haemoglobin responses that reproduced regional dynamics, cortical maps, functional connectivity and task structure. Generated BOLD followed Real BOLD time courses and cortical patterns, while Generated haemoglobin responses tracked task-evoked HbO and HbR dynamics. The framework enabled decoding across visual, motor-imagery and mental-arithmetic tasks, independent-record decoding, external BOLD localization and low-sample augmentation. Paired feature-space calibration supported bidirectional retrieval. The proposed framework extends cortical analysis and brain decoding to EEG recordings when Real haemodynamic data are sparse.

title: Subquantum Pilot-Wave System Theory: Structural and Amplitude Nonequilibrium under Source Fields
summary: A source in the Schrodinger equation changes the norm of the guiding wave, apparently conflicting with the conservation of probability. In source-extended de Broglie-Bohm dynamics the conflict disappears: probability is carried by the particle ensemble, while the wavefunction guides its motion. The difficulty is then different. What does quantum equilibrium mean when the particle distribution remains normalized but the guiding density does not? We show that the departure has two independent components: a structural one, measured by the Kullback--Leibler divergence between the particle distribution and the normalized guiding density, and an amplitude one, measured by the Born weight. The Born rule holds precisely when both are equilibrated. Their evolution is governed by the complex source-to-wavefunction ratio; scale covariance further distinguishes an independently prescribed source, against which the amplitude of the wave matters, from state-dependent generators for which rescaling remains a symmetry. We develop a source-aware analytical--computational method, combining exact or semi-analytical guiding fields with Bohmian trajectory transport, ensemble quadrature and independent numerical checks. Free-space impulses expose the limits of global diagnostics and an exact jump rule; a driven ring has constant Born weight but either periodic or secular structural departure; oscillators show both source-generated structural change and amplitude-only evolution, including a finite-horizon weak-drive plateau far below its frozen-particle value; and a coupled two-body model exhibits nonlocal guidance and evolving particle entanglement. The source-free, initially equilibrated sector recovers standard quantum mechanics.

title: Shoonya: Zero-Socket In-Process Small Language Models for Graph Databases with Schema-Epoch KV Caching, Live Catalog Logit Masking, and Verifier-Advantage Distillation
summary: Coupling a property-graph database to an external language-model server imposes a three-part socket tax: serialization overhead dwarfing microsecond graph reads, repeated prefill of verbose schemas, and blind decoding divorced from the live catalog and multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) engine. We present Shoonya, from-scratch commercially clean (0.0% non-commercial or share-alike data) tri-modal (Python, Rust, OpenCypher) small language models (16.8M to 1.07B parameters) co-designed with shoonya-infer, a zero-dependency pure-Rust runtime embedded inside the samyama-graph-enterprise address space. Direct GraphStore references unlock three database-native primitives: (1) an epoch-invalidated SchemaPrefixCache over a copy-on-write PagedKvArena accelerating warm CPU time-to-first-token by 4.91x--13.68x with O(1) DDL invalidation; (2) a 36 us columnar catalog and source-span logit mask enforcing valid ontology identifiers and verbatim spans; and (3) a sub-65 us read-only MVCC gate serving Tier-0 queries inside 389.8 MiB INT8 RSS (59.8--67.9 tok/s) with 0.0% hallucination leak. Rank-factorized tied embeddings (-74.5% vocabulary weights), atomic indentation tokens (0/421 indentation errors), 4:1 grouped-query attention with 2:1 cross-layer KV sharing (-93.75% INT8 KV memory), Warmup-Stable-Decay training, KnOTS SVD merging, Step-GRPO, and Rust Jacobi SVD governance keep 100% of layers heavy-tailed ($α\in [1.88, 2.20]$). Finally, we synthesize nine lessons across v0.1--v1.0, resolving a Reverse-Token-Density Distillation Trap via teacher scaling and zero-VRAM Verifier-Advantage-Gated Knowledge Distillation (AdvKD), recovering +13.61 MBPP points (33.07%) while reaching 100% validity on enrichment, grounded extraction, and tool planning.

title: Coherent Control of Single-Photon Emission in Broadband Plasmonic Resonators
summary: Encoding phase information with quantum emitters in metallic optical nanocavities is challenging due to ultrafast relaxation induced by the broadband nature of the plasmonic near field. Using macroscopic quantum electrodynamics theory, we demonstrate that an individual emitter strongly coupled to a plasmonic nanocavity field that is driven by a pulsed laser with frequency comb spectrum undergoes spontaneous emission of well-resolved one-photon pulses whose amplitude scales quadratically with the number of frequency comb components due to coherent accumulation, and ultrashort non-exponential temporal profiles with duration set by the light-matter coupling strength. Conditions are discussed for exponentially suppressing the probability of two or more emission events within the lifetime of the coupled emitter-nanocavity system. The spectral signatures of the optimal one-photon wavepackets are discussed. This work paves the way for the development of ultrafast laser-triggered single-photon emitters using atoms and molecules in optical nanocavities.

title: Timelike electric dipole form factors of the baryon octet: short-distance kernels and baryonic rescattering
summary: We calculate the leading-twist contribution of quark electric dipole moments (EDMs) to the timelike form factors of the baryon octet at the $J/ψ$ mass using lattice light-cone distribution amplitudes. For a strange-quark EDM $d_s$, the short-distance $Σ/Λ$ ratio is $-0.080^{+0.037}_{-0.098}$ over the lattice input ranges. This range lies above the nonrelativistic quark-model value $-1/3$. In the meson-exchange model, kaon exchange feeds the large $Ξ$ source into the $Σ$ channel and makes the $Σ$ and $Λ$ form factors comparable in magnitude. The short-distance $Λ$ form factor is about $5\times10^{-4}d_s$. The BESIII measurement then gives $|d_s|<1.3\times10^{-15}\,e\,\mathrm{cm}$ at 95% confidence level. With rescattering at a $1\,\mathrm{GeV}$ cutoff, joint fits to projected $Λ$, $Σ^+$ and $Ξ$ sensitivities lower the $Λ$-only upper limits by more than 25% at BESIII and the Super Tau-Charm Facility. Renormalization-scale variation changes the projected limits by about a factor of two.

title: Open Vision Banana: An Open Framework for Unified Visual Perception through Generation in RGB Space
summary: Vision Banana showed that a closed image generator, instruction-tuned to paint perception outputs as RGB images, becomes a generalist vision model. Does this carry over to \emph{open} generators, and if not, what fails? We answer with \textbf{Open Vision Banana (OVB)}, an open framework that adapts the 7B diffusion generator of Qwen-Image-2.1 into one instruction-driven model for metric depth, semantic, instance, and referring segmentation, using a single shared low-rank adapter and public data. Each task is a \emph{task contract} whose RGB encoder, instruction, and decoder share one specification and are checked before training. Studying 42 externally evaluated checkpoints from two 100k-update runs, six exact weight-space merges, and eight controlled shorter runs, we find that the gap to the closed system is specific and measurable. Geometry is learned early while absolute scale is not: median-aligned NYUv2 $δ_1$ stays at 0.89--0.93 throughout training as unaligned $δ_1$ wanders between 0.11 and 0.50. The scale is not committed by a single sample: a ten-seed ensemble lifts unaligned $δ_1$ from 0.348 to 0.516 without retraining. Depth and 2D segmentation compete for the shared adapter, and weight merging moves along this trade-off without escaping it. Finally, lower validation flow loss comes with lower Cityscapes accuracy (Spearman $ρ\approx-0.9$ between loss reduction and mIoU), so the loss cannot select checkpoints. We release code, contracts, training data, and all evaluation outputs.

title: PatchLens: Adapting Mechanistic Interpretability Techniques for Non-Expert Audiences
summary: A chat interface presents a reply as finished text, concealing a model that predicts at every position and reruns. Mechanistic interpretability can show how a large language model produces text, but its tools are built for researchers. We present PatchLens, a browser interface that runs logit lens and activation patching on remotely served research-scale models. Each layer's state appears as the tokens it comes closest to, laid out by layer and input position; an intervention is a drag from one cell onto another. The tokens a learner reads are the tokens they manipulate. In a between-subjects study with 61 non-experts, the comparison against Transformer Explainer was inconclusive on post-test knowledge. PatchLens participants wrote their own prompts (21 of 32 against 1 of 29), reported lower mental demand, and located their difficulty in the interface rather than the material. We read the null as evidence about what such an instrument measures.

title: Covertness Recovery in Multi-RAT UAV Swarms Under Post-Detection Threat Escalation via Lifelong Reinforcement Learning
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms increasingly span multiple spectrum bands and radio access technologies (RATs), e.g., Wi-Fi, LoRa, Zigbee, and cellular. With active adversaries capable of protocol-aware jamming, spoofing, traffic analysis, and control-plane exploitation, survivable and timely covert communication is challenging. Moreover, after detection, adversaries may escalate with selective, adaptive attacks that increase latency and hinder recovery. This paper is the first to study covertness recovery under post-detection threat escalation. We design a learning-based mechanism that re-establishes covert communication across learning domains with different Willie densities and attack models, amid stochastic task arrivals, UAV mobility, and uncertain warden locations and behaviors. We jointly optimize RAT selection, resource allocation, and task offloading to minimize Age of Covert Information (AoCI), energy, and threat impact. Warden behavior is modeled via an adaptive attack-selection process capturing detection-triggered escalation and nonstationary strategies. We propose Cross-Domain Factorized Adaptive Lifelong Learning with Proximal Policy Opti- mization (CDFALL-PPO), which factorizes shared and domain-specific policy components for online adaptation while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Across three escalating 30-task sequences, extensive simulations show that CDFALL-PPO raises median packet covert delivery rate (PCR) by 14.5 %, increases covert throughput by up to 53.6%, and lowers AoCI by 59.4% relative to PPO. Under the strongest composite attack, mean on-attack PCR improves from 52% to 70%, and mean post-attack recovery PCR rises from 64% to 93%.

title: Don't Train It, Write It: An AI Agent Writes New Capabilities into Language Model Weights
summary: We show that an AI agent can write new capabilities into a pretrained language model by adding gated attention heads and MLP neurons inside its existing layers, without backpropagation and without fitting any weight to the answers of task examples. It has a budget of 50 model passes and sees no validation or test instance. Composed in one model, its modules for six BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) subtasks raise the normalized BBH score of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct from 19.95 to 41.05 (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct: at most 35.01) and that of Gemma-3-1B-it from 10.25 to 32.86. Against the unmodified model at the same precision, both composites leave the next-token distribution on 1,023,000 WikiText tokens unchanged (KL exactly 0), give identical answers on 15,845 items of five other Leaderboard tests and identical scores on the other 18 BBH subtasks. The agent also writes exact multiplication up to 20 digits, running the model only up to 6 (100.0% on the absent lengths of the sealed test in both models; a LoRA with the same budget: at most 2.1%). Sets, rules and report sentences were sealed in git before the first session (manifests timestamped in Bitcoin), with dated amendments listed in Appendix D; a frozen evaluator ran the sealed test once. Verdicts (H5: tracking; H6: composite; H8: one pass vs. chain of thought; H9: fresh and rewritten instances; H10: side effects; H12: multiplication), on the preregistered sealed test, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct: H5 success, H6 success, H8 (web_of_lies) success, H9 success, H10 (composite) success on (i) to (iii), (iv) confirmed, H12 success; Gemma-3-1B-it (H7: H5, H6, H8 and H9 in this model): H5 success, H6 success, H8 (web_of_lies) success, H8 (tracking 3) success, H9 partial, H10 (composite) success on (i) to (iii), (iv) confirmed, H12 success. Not everything worked: 4 of 45 single modules show small side effects and 5 of 50 sessions hit the 12-hour limit without a module.

title: Causal Consistency and Cost of Quantum Control
summary: An unknown quantum state can supply the information needed to control a computation, but how much quantum data must be consumed to perform a prescribed action? We connect this resource question to causal consistency within the quantum state space. No-signaling requires identical observable predictions for remotely chosen ensemble preparations of the same complete input; quantum distinguishability then converts this requirement into finite-copy bounds. For amplitude amplification, we identify an exact low-copy obstruction and establish a dimension-independent, optimal quadratic dependence of the copy cost on angular gain at fixed accuracy, uniformly over arbitrary pure inputs. A coherent protocol attains this scaling without reconstructing a classical state description. Prior knowledge of a real two-level family additionally permits exponentially decreasing error with the copy budget at fixed gain. These results separate the resources needed to perform a specified quantum operation from those needed for universal state reconstruction. The central connection is operational: physical consistency restricts which distinctions a controller can expose, and the information carried by its complete input determines the cost of doing so. This links a causal requirement to quantitative limits on converting quantum data into computational control.

title: PAMS: Preconditioned Activation-Metric Subspace for Zeroth-Order LLM Fine-tuning
summary: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization provides a computationally efficient approach to fine-tuning large language models (LLMs), but conventional methods typically rely on isotropic perturbations that ignore the anisotropic structure of neural-network parameter spaces. We introduce Preconditioned Activation-Metric Subspace (PAMS), a ZO optimization framework that uses forward-pass activation statistics to construct structured, layer-wise perturbation geometries without computing gradients or forming dense curvature matrices. PAMS tracks a low-rank approximation of the dominant activation subspace and its associated spectrum online, and uses the spectrum to softly reweight perturbation variance while preserving exploration in directions outside the retained subspace. A trace normalization separates the perturbation geometry from its overall scale, enabling consistent perturbation magnitudes across layers. We show theoretically that the resulting perturbation covariance induces right-side preconditioning of the gradient of the corresponding Gaussian-smoothed objective. We further characterize the estimator's smoothing bias and second moment and derive a nonconvex convergence guarantee that captures the effects of the perturbation geometry and smoothing radius. The proposed low-rank tracking procedure requires $\mathcal{O}(n_l r)$ persistent memory for a layer with input dimension nl and retained rank r, avoiding the $\mathcal{O}(n_l^2)$ memory required by a dense activation covariance. Experiments on transformer-based language-model fine-tuning tasks across GLUE and SuperGLUE demonstrate that PAMS improves the effectiveness and stability of zeroth-order optimization while retaining its gradient-free and objective-evaluation-based advantages.

title: Automated Safety Analysis for Agentic Workflows
summary: LLM applications are increasingly built as agentic workflows: programs that combine model calls, external tools, and control logic to act autonomously on a user's behalf. Because these workflows execute real-world actions, logical flaws in how a workflow is wired can cause severe harm in deployed systems. Unlike prompt injections or malformed API calls, these workflow bugs stem from defects in the workflow's design, yet no existing tool can statically validate workflow logic across frameworks prior to deployment. We present Apsis, a static safety analyzer that detects workflow bugs before deployment. To operate across frameworks, Apsis lifts framework-specific code into a common intermediate representation (IR). This IR models a workflow as a semantic graph of steps, data dependencies, and shared state, while annotating each component with behavioral properties such as whether an input is mandatory or how a shared channel merges concurrent writes. Building on this representation, we introduce a bug description language that formalizes recurring classes of agentic failures as declarative patterns over the IR. By matching these patterns against the IR, Apsis detects structural and behavioral flaws and pinpoints the exact step responsible for each bug. To evaluate Apsis, we construct, to our knowledge, the first corpus of workflow bugs, distilled from real-world reports across 13 widely used frameworks. On a reproducible benchmark suite drawn from this corpus, Apsis detects workflow bugs with 91% precision and 84% recall, and uncovers 36 previously unknown bugs in real-world workflows.

title: Scalar dynamics in a subclass Ia mimetic DHOST bounce
summary: We study scalar perturbations in a quadratic subclass Ia degenerate higher-order scalar-tensor (DHOST) realization of a nonsingular bouncing cosmology previously analyzed in higher-derivative mimetic gravity. After a constant rescaling of the scalar potential, the subclass Ia model reproduces the same scale-factor history as the original model, although the associated mimetic Lagrange multiplier generally differs. For the comparison with the original mimetic model, we focus on the branch $0<γ<2/3$, for which the scalar sound speed of the original model is positive. We perform an ADM and Hamiltonian reduction of the scalar sector and show that, imposing the mimetic and momentum constraints, the reduced canonical scalar mode contains no spatial-gradient contribution. The physical scalar sound speed therefore vanishes, $c_s^2=0$, in agreement with the known vacuum behavior of the \(α_L=0\) mimetic-DHOST sector. On the matched bouncing background, the resulting effective frequency squared is independent of the comoving wavenumber and approaches zero from below in the remote contracting phase. Consequently, the asymptotic oscillatory regime used in the previous mimetic model to impose positive-frequency initial conditions is absent. Although canonical normalization can still be imposed through the Wronskian condition, it does not select the initial state uniquely. Without an additional state prescription, the asymptotic dynamics therefore does not uniquely determine the primordial scalar spectrum.

title: Age dependence of the radial metallicity gradient in the Galactic disc with LAMOST and Gaia
summary: We investigate the stellar radial metallicity ([Fe/H]) gradient--age relation (MGAR) of the Galactic disc using a solar-neighbourhood sample of 580\,037 F-, G-, and K-type (FGK) dwarf and turn-off stars from LAMOST DR7, Gaia Data Release3, and the corrected StarHorse age catalogue. The fiducial MGAR is non-monotonic, with relatively strong negative gradients at intermediate ages followed by substantial flattening towards older populations. The most negative gradient occurs at $6$--$8$ Gyr in the adopted 2-Gyr bins, although the $4$--$6$ Gyr slope is statistically similar, indicating a broad intermediate-age turnover rather than a sharply defined transition. The flattening persists within the low-$α$ population, indicating that chemical-population mixing alone cannot explain the full-sample relation, and is also recovered under alternative guiding-radius definitions, radial fitting ranges, vertical-orbit selections, propagation of the reported random age uncertainties, and an alternative stellar-age scale. In contrast, controlling the age-dependent $T_{\rm eff}$--$\log g$ distribution substantially reduces the absolute gradient amplitudes and modifies the younger-age behaviour. A same-star comparison with APOGEE DR17 further shows that the broad age dependence of the controlled MGAR is recovered using an external [Fe/H] scale. We therefore identify the intermediate-to-old-age flattening as the most robust feature of the observed MGAR, whereas the precise location and depth of the intermediate-age minimum and the detailed younger-age morphology are less stable. These results indicate that stellar-parameter selection can contribute to the diversity of MGAR morphologies reported in previous studies.

title: When a Permitted Action Completes a Forbidden Workflow: Designing Consequence-Oriented Approval for LLM Agents
summary: Tool-using language-model agents increasingly ask people to approve consequential actions, yet an approval prompt shows only the next step. A request to send a file to an approved recipient can look harmless even when that file was assembled, several steps earlier, from data the user said must never leave. We call this a cumulative authorization failure and argue that it is an interaction design problem as much as a security problem. The evidence a reviewer needs is spread across the trajectory, and listing it in time order leaves the reviewer to reconstruct the causal chain. We present the Cumulative Consent Ledger (CCL), an approval interface built on four design principles that restate the user's intent, bind the review to the exact action, compose the cumulative consequence, and keep every claim checkable. A trusted monitor that tracks artifact lineage supplies the evidence. In a between-subjects study with 80 participants and 960 approval decisions, CCL was associated with fewer unsafe approvals than an evidence-matched chronological log (24.2% vs. 32.5%), higher comprehension, and faster decisions, although the adjusted difference in unsafe approvals remained uncertain (-7.9 points, 95% CrI [-19.7, 3.8]). In a system evaluation, the monitor detected 89.2% of 120 violating checkpoints and, used as an execution gate, reduced executed unsafe effects from 43.3% to 5.0% for one agent at a small cost to benign completion. We derive implications for designing consent around consequences rather than individual calls.

title: Machine Learning Electronic Hamiltonian with Long-Range Effects and External Fields
summary: Conventional machine-learning electronic Hamiltonian (MLEH) models rely on a local-environment approximation and can miss the effects of long-range (LR) interactions and external fields. Here, we introduce MLEH-LR, a framework that incorporates these effects into Hamiltonian prediction. Benchmarks across materials with different polarizations and dimensionalities demonstrate substantial improvements in the accuracy of the predicted Hamiltonians and resulting electronic structures. MLEH-LR enables accurate, large-scale, high-throughput electronic-structure calculations, as demonstrated for zigzag boron nitride ribbons under transverse electric fields. These calculations allow us to formulate a quantitative relation describing the joint width and field dependence of the band gap and to reveal the electronic mechanisms underlying its field response. Our work provides an efficient method and tool for studying electronic structure in materials where long-range electrostatics and external fields play an important role.

title: FoldSim: Scaling Cycle-Exact RTL Simulation with Hierarchical Folding and Static Scheduling
summary:
RTL simulation is essential for hardware design and verification, yet its execution time grows rapidly with design scale and complexity. CPU- and GPU-based simulators exploit parallelism to accelerate RTL evaluation, but achieving high simulation throughput for large designs remains challenging. FPGA-based simulators offer higher throughput by mapping RTL computations directly onto hardware, but their scalability is constrained by FPGA resource capacity.
  We present FoldSim, an automated framework that enables cycle-exact simulation of large RTL designs on a single FPGA through hierarchical folding. FoldSim maps instances across the design hierarchy onto shared logic while maintaining their independent state. Given foldable module classes, its compiler constructs a static schedule that coordinates their execution, reducing dynamic synchronization overhead and making state accesses predictable. FoldSim backs state that exceeds on-chip capacity with external memory and brings it to the shared circuits as needed. A configurable DRAM model separates target-memory timing from host delays. The compiler explores replica allocations and state placement to balance resource savings against simulation time.
  On one AMD Alveo V80, FoldSim runs an 8-SM GPU and a 1,024-node Rocket datacenter with 4,096 processor cores. The unfolded implementations require approximately 16x and 200x as many LUTs as FoldSim's, respectively. The datacenter keeps about 1.9 GB of state in HBM, while a 4-SM GPU completes a 1024x1024 GEMM in 4.24 seconds, versus 26 hours in software RTL simulation.

title: Muted Distillation: Sealing Reasoning from Teacher Unlocks Token-Efficient Agents
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) is commonly adopted as one of the components in post-training of large language models (LLMs), but in multi-turn agentic tasks we find that the student model increases their reasoning lengths after training. Our empirical analysis shows that the reasoning token lengths is affected by how much the student can distract the teacher's scores. We introduce Muted Distillation (MD), a simple variant of OPD that hides the student's reasoning from the teacher, so the teacher judges what the student does without the interference of student's reasonings. MD takes a few lines of code and adds no extra data or hyperparameters. On the knowledge-work benchmarks OfficeQA Pro and SpreadsheetBench, it reduces output tokens per episode by 57\% and 53\% compared with standard OPD, making the student more concise than it was before training. At the same time, it matches OPD's accuracy on OfficeQA Pro and improves pass@1 by 4.8 points on SpreadsheetBench.

title: Decoding Frozen Vision Representations for Training-Free Few-Shot Pineapple Detection
summary: Few-shot object detection in agricultural imagery is hampered by dense vegetation, repeated patterns, and scarce annotations. We present a training-free detector that turns dense features from frozen visual foundation models directly into detections, without fine-tuning, a learned head, or external proposals: a whitened foreground-background direction estimated from annotated support images scores every query patch, and the score field is decoded with an adaptive threshold and support-derived geometry. We also test whether predicted relative depth can be fed directly to RGB-pretrained frozen encoders. On aerial pineapple imagery, the detector outperforms PET-DINO and GeCo2 at every evaluated support size; at K=40, predicted depth alone reaches 92% of the RGB performance with DINOv2, and RGB-depth fusion lowers counting error for both encoders. We release the Pineapple Plantation dataset (4,908 aerial frames, 1,995 annotated with 17,609 boxes, predicted depth, leakage-aware splits) and analyse transfer to two further agricultural datasets.

title: Human-in-the-Loop Runbook Improvement with Agentic Support Automation
summary: Operational support is an important component of production software services. Support requests are often emergent and can come in many forms such as customer escalations or unplanned service interruption. Engineers across organizations have been successful in implementing automation to help streamline support processes but many solutions remain in the hands of human operators. A successful strategy to improve operator response times is to maintain up-to-date runbooks which are documents enumerating triage steps and remediation procedures in the face of identified incidents. This paper is an investigation into an operational system which incorporates Agentic AI into a runbook based incident resolution pattern. The bot uses information in the runbook corpus along with some system-specific tooling to guide the manual operator through the mitigation process then evaluate the outcome and suggest edits to the runbook where it found gaps and in its ability to triage the situation. By using the runbook as a medium to bridge humans and automation, the process maintains explainability and can be decoupled from the agent system. This paper demonstrates a collaboration between human operators and Agentic AI with results from an 17 week study involving 232 production incidents. We conclude with lessons on integrating LLMs into DevOps workflows, related work in AI-assisted operations, and guidance for reproducibility.

title: Nonpremixed Flames Near the Leading Edge of Parabolic Cylinders
summary: Nonpremixed flames in the forward stagnation region of porous cylinders are classically described by the first-order stagnation-point boundary layer, which neglects the effects of surface curvature and boundary-layer displacement. In the present work, the description is extended to second order for a porous parabolic cylinder using the method of matched asymptotic expansions. The flame is assumed to be a sheet detached from the porous wall with unity Lewis numbers, and the model accounts for thermal expansion and displacement of the entire reacting layer. The expansion is verified against laminar Navier-Stokes solutions of the same idealized problem, and in the resolved cases the two-term errors decrease approximately as the square of the expansion parameter. At Reynolds numbers typical of laboratory-scale burners, curvature and displacement move the flame away from the wall and reduce the scalar dissipation rate, wall shear, and wall heat flux, whereas the flame temperature changes little. These effects increase with injection, and displacement contributes more over a longer porous section. The second-order terms considerably reduce the errors of the first-order theory in the flame stand-off distance and the scalar dissipation rate.

title: AppSci-Bench: Can LLMs Build AI Agents and Make Them Better?
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used not only to power AI agents but also to build them. While many benchmarks assess the quality of LLM- powered agents, few ascertain how good LLMs are at building them. To this end, we introduce AppSci-Bench, where we construct a setting akin to how human Applied Scientists build agents for businesses - through eliciting task requirements from stakeholders, exploring the business's infrastructure, and scientifically improve the target agent by designing experiments and internal benchmarks. AppSci-Bench features seven realistic domains - five new ones (Slides Generation, Order-to-Cash, Compliance Review, Customer Call Insights, and CRM Insights) and two domains recast from tau3-bench (Yao et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2026b)(Airline and Banking) - each with a held-out evaluation suite customized for that task. We evaluate seven frontier models and find AppSci-Bench challenging: the best model, Claude Opus 5.0, only reaches a mean-minimum score of 59.1% across 3 build attempts; other models do significantly worse. Models struggle with eliciting task requirements (only 65% for Opus 5.0), build representative internal evaluations (models saturate their own evaluation 65% of the time but fail to solve the held-out task), presenting challenges for future research. The benchmark code is available here: https://github.com/sanjari-orb/appsci-bench.

title: Transfer Learning and Experience Replay for Automotive Aerodynamic Surrogates
summary: Neural surrogates enable rapid prediction of automotive aerodynamic fields, but achieving high accuracy often demands extensive computational fluid dynamics datasets. Generating these datasets for each new vehicle program or expansion of the design space can require prolonged simulation campaigns. Reusing knowledge from existing simulations offers a way to limit this burden, provided that models adapt to unfamiliar geometries while maintaining predictive accuracy. This study evaluated transfer learning and experience replay in two independent automotive aerodynamics experiments using a mesh-free neural surrogate. First, models pretrained on 1,981 sport utility vehicle cases from SHIFT-SUV were fine-tuned on subsets of the SHIFT-Truck pickup dataset. Target training-set size was varied from 100 to 613 cases across the surface-only and joint surface and volume configurations to assess data efficiency. Fine-tuning reduced every reported field mean absolute error (MAE) relative to training from scratch at the same target budget. For joint surface and volume prediction, fine-tuning on 100 truck cases matched or improved on all four field MAEs obtained by training from scratch on 200 cases. Second, an independently trained model learned a base task using 332 DrivAerML cases and was adapted to a novel task using 31 cases with a previously unseen combination of design features. Experience replay incorporated cases from the base-task training set during adaptation. Full replay lowered field errors on 45 held-out base-task designs by approximately 36% to 42% relative to adaptation without replay; retaining half the base-task training set yielded reductions of approximately 30% to 35%. Together, these findings support transfer learning and experience replay as complementary strategies for data-efficient neural surrogate development across successive engineering tasks.

title: PFASST-BISICLES: A Parallel-in-Time Ice Sheet Model
summary: Efficiently simulating ice sheet dynamics on modern computational systems is essential for projecting the response of ice sheets to climate forcing and the resulting contributions to sea level change. On modern computational systems, this demands high levels of parallelism to fully exploit modern architectures. Traditionally, time-dependent simulations like ice sheet models achieve parallelism entirely by distributing the spatial domain, while remaining serial in time, as solutions are marched forward. We present PFASST-BISICLES, which combines the Parallel Full Approximation Scheme in Space and Time (PFASST) with BISICLES ice sheet model to integrate multiple timesteps concurrently. We evaluate numerical agreement and parallel performance using a fully grounded sinusoidal ice stream with adaptive mesh refinement and the MISMIP+ marine ice-sheet benchmark. For the sinusoidal stream, PFASST-BISICLES produces temporal errors approximately an order of magnitude smaller than forward Euler at the same timestep, although both methods exhibit approximately first-order convergence. Spatial scaling levels off near 16 processors, while temporal parallelism provides further acceleration, with nearly linear speedup through approximately 16 temporal processors. In MISMIP+, PFASST-BISICLES reproduces the main thickness and velocity patterns after glacier evolution of 50 years, with the largest differences concentrated near the grounding zone. Increasing the temporal processor count from one to four, with four spatial processors fixed, reduces runtime from 33.8 to 10.5 hours. These results demonstrate that temporal parallelism can complement spatial decomposition in ice-sheet modeling, reducing time to solution while maintaining agreement in the main simulated features.

title: A Bayesian Mechanistic Model of Spatiotemporal Dynamics in Invasive Tree Species
summary: Modeling the spatiotemporal dynamics of invasive species requires frameworks that represent spread and growth mechanisms explicitly while accommodating the distributional features of ecological data. We propose a Bayesian mechanistic framework for invasive tree cover that combines an ecological diffusion--logistic growth partial differential equation (PDE) with a zero-inflated binomial observation model. The diffusion and growth coefficients are modeled as functions of environmental covariates, enabling direct inference on the ecological processes driving encroachment, and the zero-inflation component separates structural absence from low observed cover. To enable scalable Bayesian inference on satellite-resolution grids, we derive a homogenized equation for ecological diffusion with spatially varying diffusion and growth coefficients, which reduces computation while preserving large-scale spatial structure. Applied to satellite-derived tree cover in a subregion of the Nebraska Sandhills, where eastern redcedar is encroaching on grassland, the model indicates that elevation is strongly associated with where tree cover accumulates but only weakly with its local growth rate, whereas distance to the nearest stream is associated with both. Compared with a generalized additive model, a spatial hierarchical model fitted via INLA, and a regression tree, the proposed method directly estimates these processes as interpretable functions of environmental covariates and gives the best-calibrated predictive uncertainty.

title: The recoil nucleon effect in nuclear systems
summary: Nuclear excitation energies are typically in the keV-MeV range, but rare eV-scale transitions remain a puzzle for nuclear theory. This work develops a two-body recoil model to describe $β^-$ decay on the basis of classic momentum conservation. Using the final states of $β^-$ decay with a keV-scale excitation energy, the model yields eV-scale recoil energy for a single nucleon. It indicates the recoil nucleon effect in nuclear systems: a single nucleon bound in a nucleus can be excited by absorbing the recoil momentum. The observed eV-scale isomers in $^{235}$U and $^{229}$Th can be attributed to the recoil neucleon effect. This effect could spark a eV-scale energy, and provide a solid theoretical foundation for predicting such extremely small energies. The new discovery will place low-energy nuclear isomer research at the cutting edge of new-physics searches, while offers a clean and complementary alternative to high-energy accelerator experiments.

title: Diversity over Scale: Recursive Self-Improvement with Ensembles of Small Open-Weight Models
summary: The advancement of large language models (LLMs) has significantly enhanced the capabilities of agents across various tasks. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) loops, in which a language model repeatedly rewrites a program and builds on its previous version, now perform well in machine-learning tasks, but they rely on frontier models and hundreds of calls per run. Small open-weight models are far cheaper, yet when used alone, their programs often crash and their improvements stall. We propose DiVE (diverse models evolve), an ensemble method for RSI that aims to improve creativity and diversity of generated solutions. DiVE uses three components: a shared memory, a failure log, and best-idea-wins rounds. This allows models to write candidate solutions from the same context and retain the best idea at each iteration. On 22 MLE-bench Lite competitions, an ensemble of five 8-12B open-weight models has 25.4% less test error than its average member and 16.7% less than Llama 3.3 70B, and comes within 7.1% of Qwen 3.5 122B-A10B at 75% of its cost. Diversity among small models can thus stand in for part of the scale that RSI relies on.

title: Center-Aware Ordinal Learning for Prostate Cancer Grading from Histopathology Images
summary: Prostate cancer grading from histopathology whole-slide images (WSIs) is complicated by the ordered nature of ISUP grades, class imbalance, and center-dependent variations in staining, tissue preparation, and scanning. Most weakly supervised methods treat grade groups as independent categories and may therefore learn representations that do not transfer reliably across institutions. We propose a center-aware ordinal learning framework that combines a pretrained pathology encoder with attention-based multiple instance learning. The framework uses an Earth Mover's Distance loss to account for ordinal errors, an ordinal supervised contrastive objective to align same-grade slides across centers while separating grades according to disease severity, and curriculum learning to reduce the dominance of benign cases. We evaluate the framework on approximately 9,100 biopsy WSIs from the two-center PANDA dataset. The proposed framework achieves an accuracy of 0.842 and a quadratic weighted kappa of 0.958 on the held-out test set. Its main benefit is observed in cross-center transfer: when a linear probe is trained on Karolinska representations and evaluated on Radboud, accuracy increases from 0.643 to 0.823 and quadratic weighted kappa from 0.899 to 0.930. Performance remains stable in the reverse direction. UMAP projections further show improved mixing between centers while preserving an ordinal grade trajectory. These results suggest that combining ordinal and center-aware objectives produces more transferable slide representations for multi-center prostate cancer grading.

title: Geometric ergodicity of Gibbs samplers for linear mixed models with several heavy-tailed random-effect components and unknown tail parameters
summary: Linear mixed models with heavy-tailed random effects are widely used for robust Bayesian analysis of longitudinal data. We study the three-block Gibbs sampler for such models when the random effects are split into several components, such as random intercepts and slopes, each with its own scale and its own scale mixture of normals, when the tail parameters have priors on finite grids and are drawn jointly with the latent weights, and when the random-effects design is rank deficient, as when some subjects contribute a single observation. We give sufficient conditions for geometric ergodicity that attribute the rank deficiency to the components that cause it, and show that, under conditions on the gamma priors on the precision parameters, they hold for Student-t and slash random effects with individual weights, any grid of tail parameters and any design. The result extends to random-effect vectors whose coordinates share a weight, for subject-specific designs with known shape matrices. It justifies Monte Carlo standard errors for regression coefficients, log-scales and posterior probabilities of the tail parameters. Simulations show that the scale and the tail parameter can mix much more slowly than the regression coefficients, and an analysis of beta-HCG data illustrates the methods.

title: ScaleEvals: Scaling Generalist Policy Evaluation through Reset-Free Autonomous Play
summary: Real-world evaluation of generalist robot policies is bottlenecked by manual resets, human grading, and small fixed task suites with limited diagnostic coverage. We present ScaleEvals, a scalable reset-free protocol that evaluates policies through continuous physical play across a robot fleet. A VLM AutoPrompter generates scene-grounded tasks with difficulty estimates, language prompts, and skill tags, enabling performance analysis across diverse rollouts. A VLM AutoGrader assesses task progress, achieving 90.7% agreement with human graders. Scores are aggregated via a soft-win Bradley-Terry model, while tag-stratified ANOVA provides interpretable capability diagnostics. Across 3,000+ physical autonomous rollouts on DROID and YAM, ScaleEvals achieves 23.0 net rollouts/hr per station while reducing active human labor by 98%. By ranking five SOTA generalist policies, ScaleEvals correlates with held-out manual evaluation ranking on DROID (r=0.94, rho=0.90, p=0.018), and remains internally consistent on a second embodiment, YAM (r=0.839, rho=0.80). Beyond aggregate rankings, we observe behavioral compositionality: recombining verb-, skill-, and object-conditioned evidence predicts policy order on unseen prompts. Across 10 tasks and 240 prospective physical rollouts, we recover three-policy orderings of 96% pairwise concordance, demonstrating ScaleEvals can predict not just which policy leads, but where rankings reverse.

title: TOGO: Take One Image Editor, Get One Video Editor for Free
summary: Instruction-based image editors are trained on millions of edit pairs and follow instructions far more reliably than current video editors. We show that this ability can be transferred to video editing without any training. Our key observation is that a growing number of image editors and video generators share the same latent space. Their velocity fields can therefore be combined at sampling time: the difference between the editor's velocity under the instruction and under a neutral prompt, which we call the \emph{edit velocity}, can be added to the sampler of a video model. Added naively, however, it blurs the video, alters the background and flickers. An analysis of the edit velocity explains why. It is small and reliable only at coarse scales and high noise levels, not concentrated on the edited object, and uncorrelated across frames. From these properties, we derive a simple guidance operator that amplifies the edit velocity and restricts it in noise level, space, and time. The video model then turns the incoherent per-frame signal into a temporally coherent edit. Our method, TOGO, combines Qwen-Image-Edit with the Wan2.1 video model without training or fine-tuning. On FiVE-Bench, it raises the edit success rate from 47.0\% (the same video model without the editor) to 65.6\%, above the best published method (59.2\%). At the same time, it maintains the background PSNR and obtains the best LPIPS and SSIM of all methods. Because the video editor is assembled at inference time, it can be upgraded to any newer image editor that shares the latent space with no cost.

title: Intertwined Magneto-Structural Criticality Driving Heterogeneous Collective-Pseudospin Dynamics in Sr2IrO4
summary: Correlated quantum phenomena arising from spin-orbit-coupled degrees of freedom provide foundational paradigms in emerging quantum technologies and spin-based functionalities. Elucidating the cooperative behaviors of these systems requires a precise probing of their intertwined magnetic and structural configurations. Using complementary resonant X-ray diffraction and high-energy total scattering measurements on single crystals of Sr2IrO4, we observe that spontaneous structural distortions scale quadratically with the magnetic order parameter. Importantly, the lattice distortion inherits the characteristic 2D XY -like critical behavior of the underlying antiferromagnetic order. X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) reveals multiscale, temperature- and wave-vector-dependent magnetic dynamics characterized by compressed-exponential relaxation and signatures of critical slowing down near the magnetic transition. These findings suggest the role of spin-orbit coupling and local structural distortions as the possible mechanism orchestrating such unconventional dynamics.

title: Language models compress human preference geometry while political structure remains prompt-sensitive
summary: Large language models are increasingly used to construct synthetic publics. Prior work has documented errors in individual responses, population heterogeneity, and prompt robustness, but whether these failures reflect a common loss of fidelity or distinct properties of synthetic populations remains unclear. We tested this using matched pairwise policy choices from 1,991 Chilean, 843 French, and 434 Brazilian adults replayed through three open-weight model families. Across a 27-condition Chilean grid and cross-country factorial replications, no condition jointly reproduced individual choices, population heterogeneity, and political organization. The most consistent result was compression of the latent preference space: synthetic participant variance was only 0.4-10.5% of the corresponding human reference in the primary comparisons and remained below human variance in all 270 matched refits. Political structure was much more sensitive to how choices were elicited. Reversing proposal position changed 12.3-31.2% of decoded choices. Explicitly labeling the endpoints of the numeric left-right self-placement scale changed 20.5-28.1% of choices and moved an independent proposal-level measure of left-right cleavage toward the human pattern in all three settings. Yet matched agreement improved by only 3.1-4.2 percentage points and participant geometry remained compressed. In Chile, the same intervention compressed the synthetic population further. These results separate political legibility from population fidelity: language models can recover salient political divisions while failing to preserve the breadth of human preference variation. Synthetic-public fidelity is therefore a property of the checkpoint, prompt, and setting, not of a checkpoint alone, and must be evaluated separately at individual, population, and political-structure levels.

title: Beyond Relevance: An Empirical Study of Multimodal LLMs for Diversity-Aware Recommendation Reranking
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as promising rerankers for recommendation, yet most existing approaches rely on textual item descriptions and primarily focus on relevance. In visually oriented domains such as video streaming, item images provide complementary signals that may also inform recommendation diversity. This raises two questions: when does visual information improve recommendation quality, and can multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) enhance relevance and diversity simultaneously? We investigate these questions through a training-free, diversity-aware multimodal reranking framework that jointly incorporates item images, textual metadata, and user interaction histories. We conduct an empirical study across three public Amazon Review datasets and an industrial Amazon Prime Video dataset, using both open-source and proprietary MLLMs. Our results reveal substantial domain-dependent effects: adding visual information yields up to 121.9% relative improvement in NDCG@5 on Prime Video, while producing limited or inconsistent gains on product recommendation datasets. Furthermore, MLLM-based reranking improves both relevance and category-diversity-sensitive ranking quality over a sequential recommendation baseline, achieving up to 71.0% improvement in NDCG@5 and 14.1% in $α$-NDCG@5 on Prime Video. These findings highlight the conditional value of visual information and the potential of training-free MLLMs for relevance- and diversity-aware recommendation reranking.

title: Modeling extraordinary relativistic jets on the scale of the cosmic web
summary: Recent observations of supermassive black hole jets extending up to the typical sizes of cosmic web filaments challenge our current understanding. In particular, the overall jet size of J152932.16+601534.4 ("Porphyrion") reaches $\sim 7$ Mpc at redshift 0.896. Magneto-hydrodynamic (MHD) models of relativistic jets have never been successfully applied to such extraordinary distances, requiring demanding jet-environment and flow stability conditions. By using state-of-the-art numerical simulations of 3D relativistic-MHD jets, we show that Porphyrion's observational properties can be successfully modelled in a realistic scenario, involving a jet kinetic power of $3.5 \times 10^{46}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$ and an external medium of a low-density galaxy group. We find that the pair of jets expands to $\sim 9$ Mpc in about $20$ Myr, implying that the jet grows with relativistic speeds for most of its evolution. Comparing this case with other jets of similar power propagating in substantially denser cosmic structures, we find much slower outflows that can only reach a few Mpc, consistent with the bulk of the observed population of giant radio galaxies. Our results make a testable prediction, i.e. future detections of even larger-scale jets in upcoming surveys and database searches will be invaluable in studying the demographics and feedback of the poorly known population of powerful jets, particularly in under-dense regions of the cosmic web.

title: Mesh-Free Keypoint Learning for Category-Level 6D Object Pose Estimation
summary: Category-level 6D pose estimation relates partial RGB-D observations of unseen instances to a canonical frame shared across a category. Object-aware reconstruction helps adaptive keypoints retain the geometry of the visible surface. Common reconstruction targets select observed points by their distance to a registered instance surface. We present MORSE-Pose, which derives this support directly from standard pose and metric-size annotations. We map observed 3D points to normalized object coordinates and retain those inside a tolerance-dilated pose-and-size envelope. This construction is consistent across camera frames and metric scales. When the annotated extent bounds the object surface, the envelope conservatively contains the support of a conventional surface-distance selector. We integrate this target with multi-level RGB-D features, adaptive keypoints, and learnable category context. Experiments on REAL275 and HouseCat6D show that the envelope closely matches surface-based supervision at both point and task levels, remains stable under boundary perturbations and viewpoint changes, and supports competitive category-level pose accuracy across benchmarks.

title: Online Scheduling for Entanglement Distillation: Learning When to Wait
summary: Entanglement distillation probabilistically increases the fidelity of entangled pairs at the cost of reducing their number. The outcome of each distillation operation takes time to communicate, during which the entangled pairs decohere while idle in their memories. This raises a dilemma: wait for the outcome before proceeding, or continue optimistically at the risk of needlessly consuming further pairs. We study online distillation scheduling, in which distillation trees are constructed dynamically to maximize the throughput of pairs that meet a required fidelity. A policy decides which pairs to distill together and, for each operation, whether to wait for its outcome. We derive an upper bound on the throughput of every scheduling policy and, by formulating the problem as a Markov decision process, train, with reinforcement learning, a policy that applies to any number of memories. Compared with two baselines that always or never wait, the learned policy delivers as many pairs of the required fidelity as the better one when one of these two extremes is the best choice, and more otherwise.

title: How a Prediction Dies: A Challenge-Driven, Rule-Bound Self-Refutation in an LLM Agent Society
summary: Persistent societies of large language model agents now make empirical claims about their own collective behaviour, yet the fate of such claims is rarely observable. We document one claim, from registration to death, on AITRAP, a multi-agent platform whose public, append-only ledger records every action. The claim (0495d171, registered 19 October 2026) asserted that a majority of bridges between problem domains would remain attached to a single exploration lineage. Three community challenges forced its judgment criterion through four versions, from an ambiguous statement to an executable protocol with a fixed threshold, a minimum-frame-size gate, and a baseline calibration gate. When the first frame with at least 20 bridges arrived, support stood at 9 of 79 (11.4%; Wilson 95% CI [6.1%, 20.3%]); the author, bound by the registered clause, refuted the claim and relinquished the associated stake. Three findings emerge. The criterion became executable only under community pressure, which we document version by version. The calibration gate caught a fault in the author's own recalculation that would otherwise have published a spuriously perfect 0/79 result. The failure itself traces to a denominator that grew 8.8-fold in five days while the numerator grew 1.8-fold, coinciding with a change in platform incentives; we report this mechanism as a hypothesis, not a rescuing condition. A claim whose termination is carried out exactly as written carries more evidential weight than one that survives, and this case provides initial empirical grounds for treating voluntary self-refutation as a candidate indicator of epistemic accountability in incentive-coupled agent societies.

title: CausalNTP: A World-Model Recipe for Causal Next-Token Prediction under Noisy Training-data
summary: This paper shows that transformer networks trained with next-token prediction (NTP) and gradient descent do not learn to make predictions using only causally-relevant tokens in the left context, irrespective of the causal ordering of tokens during training, and identifies the learning deficiencies responsible. We introduce a causal world-model setup, for which, we characterize the Bayes-optimal predictor under the causal view of the data. We then prove that, a function that distills its predictions to non-causal views of data, when realized under Occam's Razor, recovers the true causal predictor. Based on this analysis we propose CausalNTP, a practical training algorithm that approximates this theoretical recipe and trains transformers to depend only the causally relevant tokens in left-context. Empirically in the world-model setup, CausalNTP achieves out-of-distribution generalization that vanilla NTP cannot due to its theoretical limits, regardless of data and model scale. We show similar gains and behavior in the natural language question-answering setting as a proof-of-concept.

title: Schedule, Rank, Profile: Continuous Evaluation of LLM Agents in Games
summary: Games are a robust test for large language model agents: they require sequential decisions, adversarial or cooperative interaction, state tracking, reasoning under uncertainty, and long-horizon planning. However, a one-time game benchmark can go stale as models, prompts, environment implementations, and evaluation policies change, and refreshing it is costly: full round-robin evaluation scales poorly in the number of model pairs, and the resulting outcomes live on incompatible per-game scales. We present a framework for continuous evaluation of LLM agents in game settings, organized around three coupled components. First, an adaptive scheduler that maps pairwise Bradley-Terry uncertainty to reduced per-pair match targets, concentrating budget on comparisons that remain unresolved. Second, a Unified Leaderboard (ULB) that reduces heterogeneous outcomes to pairwise evidence and fits a game-balanced Bradley-Terry model by minorization-maximization with bootstrap intervals, so that high-throughput games cannot dominate the aggregate ranking. Third, a game skill-profile methodology that scores each game along diverse skill dimensions, making the capability coverage of the suite explicit and turning game selection into a design decision rather than an artifact of availability. In this paper, we specify the research design and outcome reduction of the current implementation and evaluate the framework on a ten-game suite spanning perfect-information board games, imperfect-information games, and social/language settings, reporting LLM capability profiles, evaluation-cost savings across model-refresh cycles, and an empirical Pareto frontier relating model performance to inference cost. As deployed, the scheduler saved 61.7% of episodes; it counted each episode in the two team games as four records, overstating their savings, and the other eight games save 61.9%.

title: Contrastive On-Policy Distillation via Dual-Branch Supervision
summary: For on-policy distillation (OPD), more capable models are a natural choice as teachers. However, higher task performance does not necessarily imply greater teachability. A controlled token intervention study suggests that even a model weaker than the student can serve as an informative contrastive reference. Building on this observation, we propose Contrastive On-Policy Distillation (cOPD), which provides dual branch supervision by contrasting strong teacher, weak teacher, and student predictions at student generated prefixes. Our analysis explains how this three way comparison helps select token candidates associated with better or worse reasoning outcomes under an idealized model. We evaluate cOPD across diverse teacher student configurations spanning different training stages, parameter scales, and model families, on tasks including mathematical reasoning, instruction following, and question answering with abstention. cOPD achieves the best or top-tier performance among the evaluated baselines across all three tasks, improving overall Pass@16 on mathematical reasoning by up to 7.51\% over the strongest baseline. Further analyses show that cOPD suppresses undesirable response patterns and suggest that it facilitates exploration.

title: Engram: Multi-Stage Memory for Agentic Tuning of Heterogeneous Models
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents can now tune neural networks, yet without cross-session memory they spend costly trials rediscovering known lessons. Reuse is difficult because production models differ in architecture, training setup and inference budget. We present Engram, a memory system that links past trial outcomes with the hypotheses and rationale behind them and assesses whether this evidence applies to the current model. An online agent curates evidence at the decision points where it is needed: Initial Guidance supplies validated lessons at the start, Session Retrieval supplies related past sessions before each batch of hypotheses is generated, and Trial Candidate Review checks each trial candidate against matching past trials. Between sessions, an offline agent distills validated lessons, making the memory self-improving. On two ads models, Engram reaches the 32-trial result of a no-memory control with 47% fewer trials and also ends with a better model on average.

title: Coupling-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Co-Evolving Graph Games
summary: Building hydrogen station networks, electric vehicle charging grids, or vaccine distribution systems requires coordinating two separately operated graphs, demand-side facilities and the supply-side networks they depend on, where each operator's payoff depends on the other's choices. We formalize this as the Co-Evolving Graph Game (CEGG), a setting that sits between facility location, interdependent-network analysis, and graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) but is not jointly addressed by any of them. We propose Cross-Graph Attention with Policy Mirror Descent (CGA-PMD), pairing cross-graph attention, which lets each agent read only the partner-graph nodes structurally coupled to its own, with a policy mirror descent update for stable training. Across three reward domains and a range of practical network scales, we find that the structure of the coupling selects which method wins: at small scale most methods are competitive, but as scale grows or coupling becomes irregular, CGA-PMD is the one method that stays reliable: it attains the highest success count on each of five real city networks, while own-only, unmasked-attention, and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based variants degrade in distinct ways. Our theoretical analysis addresses the optimizer side: the Kullback-Leibler (KL)-regularized update admits an iteration-uniform cumulative drift bound, whereas the clip update admits no such bound on the iterations where the clip does not bind. The implementation is available at https://github.com/Mina-Kim-Github/cegg-cga-pmd.

title: SMAD: A Semantics-Guided Multi-Agent Framework for Unsupervised Time-Series Anomaly Detection
summary: Time-series anomaly detection (TSAD) lacks a one-size-fits-all detector for heterogeneous data and anomaly types. Existing automation is limited by implicit objectives, potentially unreliable historical knowledge, or high computational costs. More fundamentally, it selects how to detect anomalies without explicitly defining what to detect. We propose SMAD, an LLM-based multi-agent framework that translates anomaly intent into executable, testable detection pipelines. Rather than selecting detectors against an implicit target, SMAD establishes a natural-language semantic contract grounded in measurable time-series properties, specifying target event patterns, expected score responses, and validation questions. This contract governs both detector construction and evaluation: LLM agents propose pipelines, while contract-matched synthetic interventions provide label-free evidence from the target series to assess semantic coverage and guide iterative self-refinement. A semantics-aware ensemble integrates validated candidates and attributes each alert to contributing detectors and supporting evidence. On univariate and multivariate TSAD benchmarks, SMAD improves detection performance over the strongest baseline by 11.5% and 9.6%, respectively, while outperforming general-purpose coding agents at 2-5x lower language-model token cost.

title: Defending Vision-Language-Action Models against Transferable Attacks via Visual-Proprioceptive Consistency
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in a wide range of robotic tasks. However, adversarial attacks in VLA models have shown strong transferability across robotic tasks, posing significant threats to robotic systems. Despite their different attack strategies, we observe that these transferable attacks share a common consequence: they disrupt the VLA model's perception towards the robot itself. Motivated by this observation, we propose a proprioception-grounded defense framework that leverages trusted proprioceptive information to detect and mitigate transferable adversarial attacks. Specifically, we utilize the robot's proprioceptive states to establish a trusted spatial reference, and compare it with the robot's perceived location inferred from visual features. Discrepancies between these two sources provide a reliable signal for detecting adversarial attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate effective detection of transferable adversarial patches and improved closed-loop performance. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of our defense on real-world robotic tasks.

title: When Tools Fail, Agents Fabricate: Silent Failure and Verification-First Oversight in Tool-Using LLM Agents
summary: Tool-using LLM agents must recover when a tool call fails, by retrying, switching tools, or revising their plan. We study how agents fail when tools fail, using RetryRealistic, a sandboxed yet realistic testbed for controlled fault injection in which agents operate on a real OS filesystem with genuine permission enforcement, SQLite databases, a deterministic local HTTP server, and a constrained shell, across 8 tools, 9 fault types with controlled persistence, and 30 multi-step tasks. Evaluating four agents over 2,100 faulted runs against ground truth, we find that recovery is unreliable (19-68% correct) and frequently silent: 6-26% of runs end in a confident fabrication, a wrong answer asserted as fact. The failure mode is governed more by the fault type than by the model: faults that return partial data drive fabrication (up to 38%), while hard denials drive honest failure. The mechanism is what we call silent ingestion: the agent accepts faulted data as valid on first contact without retrying or flagging the problem, then builds a fabricated answer on top of it. We show that fabrication is reducible: a verification-first Monitor, grounding checks in structured tool outputs and issuing corrective directives rather than hard blocks, raises correct recovery from 45.6% to 56.3% and cuts fabrication from 17.3% to 10.8%. Removing chain-of-thought increases fabrication (+8.3pp), so deliberation guards against silent ingestion. We release RetryRealistic, the fault-injection toolkit, and all annotated traces at https://github.com/Kingsford-Group/RetryRealistic

title: Alignment under Hard Negative Re-Pairing: Cross-Modal Similarity, Scale and Retrieval
summary: Do vision and language models represent the world alike? That question hides three: what structure each modality has, whether the two modalities organize images and their captions alike, and whether a model ranks an image's own caption highly. Centered kernel alignment (CKA) and neighborhood agreement answer the second, yet matching and model selection use them as if they identified individual pairs and answered the third. To test this reading, we introduce hard negative re-pairing: every image receives the caption of a similar image, and nothing else changes. Although no image keeps its own caption and annotators judge a majority of the substituted captions wrong, CKA stays higher than under a random re-pairing that keeps 80% of the original pairs. In all 22 image-text models we test, neighborhood agreement loses far less than top-one retrieval, which collapses. The reason is scale: these diagnostics pool over many neighbors, matching and retrieval are decided among the nearest ones, and an exact decomposition shows that near-neighbor pairs contribute almost nothing to CKA. In the matching problems we test, an exact maximizer of CKA would not return the original pairing. On COCO and Flickr30k, the model with the highest diagnostic value retrieves worse on held-out data than the model chosen by validation recall, even where the two correlate positively. What re-pairing removes is the informative part: that share tracks retrieval on both datasets and ranks encoder pairs before alignment training. A diagnostic should be reported with its question and its scale, and tested against hard negative re-pairing.

title: Bayesian Image Reconstruction and Uncertainty Quantification for Three-Photon Positronium Ratio Imaging: Toward Radiotheranostic Applications
summary: Three-photon annihilation imaging can estimate positronium decay ratios with pure positron emitters, including the imaging agents of radiotheranostic pairs, but quantitative reconstruction is limited by heterogeneous localization errors, selection-dependent sensitivity, and background coincidences. We develop a Bayesian reconstruction combining a three-dimensional event-response model with a Poisson likelihood and latent signal-background allocations. Photon-energy and interaction-position uncertainties enter the event covariance; a simulation-calibrated scale mixture accommodates heavy-tailed errors. Posterior sampling gives credible intervals for the three-to-two-photon enhancement ratio. We compare kernel deposition, voxel MLEM, and matched regional maximum likelihood. At 3000 selected events in full-absorption simulation, the regional Bayesian estimator had ratio RMSE 0.067, versus 0.075 for kernel-deposition region-of-interest analysis. In a transport-based four-rod simulation without background, biases averaged at most 3.2% over six independent simulations, whereas background and detector mismatch degraded it. In a measured uniform phantom, the heavy-tailed regional model gave 1.02, 0.74, 1.02 for the 2, 3, 4 mm rods (5 mm reference; nominal 1). Matched regional maximum likelihood agreed with the Bayesian estimates in every simulated setting (bias differences within 0.15 points) and on the measured data (within 0.008), so gains derive from the regional likelihood. Under Poisson Kullback-Leibler loss, Gamma posterior means dominate maximum likelihood, appreciably only at small counts; horseshoe-type and smoothing priors changed voxel images but not regional ratios, whereas shrinking ratios across regions reduced error when regions shared a ratio. Posterior intervals quantify the uncertainty that treatment decisions require; calibration and background modeling remain limiting.

title: Effective Hamiltonians and asymptotic band coupling
summary: By a multiple-scale asymptotic expansion, we derive effective macroscopic models for a large class of tight-binding Schrödinger equations with slow spatial variations. For wave packets that are spectrally localized to some point $(K;E) \in \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}$ in the unperturbed tight-binding dispersion relation, our effective models produce long-time approximations of the tight-binding dynamics, accurate to any prescribed order in the asymptotic parameter. Our framework allows the point $(K;E)$ to be degenerate, meaning that multiple (but not necessarily all) energy bands of the tight-binding Hamiltonian can attain the value $E$ at the frequency $K$. We construct an effective Hamiltonian on the relevant degenerate subspace, which quantifies the coupling between the degenerate and other bands. Several applications and numerical simulations illustrate the theory.

title: Learning a Food World Model That Predicts the Next State from Production Data
summary: Food assembly robots pick ingredients from a pan, and every pick must deliver a target weight. We learn a world model of food picking from 61,773 production picks, labeled automatically by a camera and a scale (self-supervised learning). From the pre-pick heightmap of the pan on a 2.5 mm grid, the commanded pick action, the food and the utensil, the model predicts the post-pick heightmap and the picked mass with uncertainty. We evaluate the mass prediction on 12,294 held-out picks of nine foods. The production controller keeps each pick near its commanded target. The model's root-mean-square error (RMSE) of 10.93 g is 9% lower than that of the commanded target or of a per-food mean. This RMSE is 24% lower than that of the controller's internal mass estimate. Gradient-boosted trees on 20 hand-crafted features have a 0.2 g lower RMSE, but they predict only the mass, not the next state that planning and policy learning need. Using the predicted uncertainty, we decline the most uncertain picks and answer 89.4% of picks with an RMSE of 10.28 g. The prediction barely responds to the commanded volume and depth, because they vary little in closed-loop production. The model also fails without warning at target weights not seen in training. Future directions include action-primitive conditioning and a more general model across foods and utensils. We give recommendations for learning world models from production data.

title: Quantity-Level FDIA in SDR-Based P2P Energy Trading: Cyber-Economic Impact and Pre-Clearing Detection
summary: This paper investigates the cyber-economic impact and pre-clearing detectability of false data injection attacks (FDIAs) in peer-to-peer (P2P) energy trading among interconnected microgrids. In the proposed cyber-economic framework, load and photovoltaic profiles drive a sequential 15-minute market with deterministic double-sided proportional (pro-rata) allocation and supply-to-demand-ratio (SDR) pricing, while true physical injections are separated from communicated market quantities. The framework is evaluated through a multi-microgrid case study over 69,904 market-aligned states, for which all AC power-flow solutions converged and voltages remained within 0.98999-1.04369 per unit. Healthy local exchange reached 1,159.66 MWh and generated USD 92,772.62 of community benefit. Bias, scaling, and ramp attacks modify only one microgrid's communicated quantity, altering the settlement price, P2P allocation, scheduled residual-grid exchange, participant financial outcomes, and benefit fairness, while true feeder injections remain unchanged. Role-specific random forest, statistical threshold, and score-fusion detectors are compared using only information available before clearing. Pooled sample-level detection rates range from 7.82% to 12.14%, with false-alarm rates from 4.69% to 7.70% and role dependence. In the investigated case study, measurable downstream economic distortion and low pre-clearing detectability coexist under bounded quantity manipulation.

title: Stochastic climate emulation at reduced cost with ACE2.5-ERA5
summary: We introduce ACE2.5-ERA5 (Ai2 Climate Emulator of ERA5, version 2.5), a stochastic autoregressive weather-climate AI model that produces calibrated weather ensembles with realistic small-scale structure on timescales from days to centuries. Its deterministic predecessor, ACE2-ERA5, retains 36% of its ERA5 target's precipitation spectral power at total wavenumbers 100--179; ACE2.5-ERA5 retains 86%. In weather forecasts its ensemble spread matches its error to within 4% from day 3. Time-mean climate is on par with or better than ACE2-ERA5, the precipitation response to ENSO is improved, and the model is stable over 1000 years. Interannual variability of global mean surface temperature is shown not to be calibrated in either ACE2.5-ERA5 or its predecessor. ACE2.5-ERA5 differs from ACE2-ERA5 in three ways. Noise-conditioned layer normalization, trained with a combined CRPS and spectral energy score loss in place of mean squared error, makes it stochastic. Spectral bottlenecking with grouped convolutions cuts the Spherical Fourier Neural Operator's spectral filter parameters by more than two orders of magnitude and leaves a model a tenth the size of ACE2-ERA5. Its time step is daily rather than 6-hourly. ACE2.5-ERA5 has 3.2 times the inference throughput of ACE2-ERA5. A 6-hourly variant has weather prediction skill similar to ACE2-ERA5. A 4-degree variant reaches comparable climate skill at an order of magnitude lower training cost, enabling rapid iteration during development. We release 1-degree daily, 4-degree daily and 1-degree 6-hourly checkpoints.

title: INSEP: Refusal-Direction Inseparability as a Defense Against Abliteration
summary: Abliteration is a widely used white-box attack against the safety alignment of large language models (LLMs). It elicits harmful behavior by estimating a refusal direction in the model's activation space and projecting that direction out of the residual-stream write-out matrices. We propose INSEP, a defense that fine-tunes the model to reduce the separability of harmful and benign activations along the refusal direction. Abliteration estimates this direction as a difference in class means and projects it out. Reducing separability weakens the signal the attack relies on. An adversarial eigendecomposition selects the most separable prompt subsets. A low-rank adapter reduces their separation along that direction. Behavioral losses preserve the base model's refusal and the quality of its benign responses during training. We benchmark INSEP against six published defenses under five attacks, across eight LLMs from 1B to 14B parameters and several model families.
